Reviewer #5:

This study shows a very striking effect of parietal tRNS on object discrimination and corresponding large changes in functional connectivity. Such data are sure to be of interest to numerous researchers due to their practical significance. That said, I have statistical concerns and am left wanting more mechanistic insight. Ultimately, I think more data and analyses will be needed to make a convincing enough case to the readership of this outlet.

1) The effect of parietal tRNS on object discrimination is truly massive. The tasks are titrated at the start to set performance at 50%. While performance remains the same following temporal and sham tRNS, parietal tRNS improves performance by 30%. Given this finding, I am rather convinced that parietal tRNS improves object discrimination. What I am not convinced of is that the effect size is as massive as is being depicted. Given that the main contribution of this study as it is current written is practical, having a reasonable estimate of effect size is important for applied work that will seek to build on this striking finding. However, given the small sample size (10 participants per group), and effect size inflation that occurs when conditionalizing on significance, especially in small samples, I suspect that the true effect size is substantially smaller than has been depicted. Unfortunately, I do not see a good way to get a better estimate of the true effect size without acquiring more data. The upshot is that new data would not require fMRI and may not even require control groups. A bare minimum would be to collect another group of 10 participants receiving parietal tRNS and estimate effect size based on their improvement. I think that such data collection would be a low cost effort, and the sample size is small enough to potentially be feasible amidst pandemic restrictions. Note that since the new sample would be used to estimate effect size, there need not be statistically significant improvement in the new sample to have utility.

2) These data beg the question of why parietal tRNS produces such a dramatic effect, but temporal tRNS does not. That is, one would like to have some mechanistic insight into why parietal tRNS is so effective, at least in the object discrimination task. The connectivity data do not, in their present form, address this question. They merely provide another metric of change without begetting further causal inference/insight. Fortunately, the authors have additional task fMRI data that could potential shed some light on the issue. For example, one might ask whether the extent to which a given task activates the stimulated areas is associated with changes in connectivity and/or behavior. Alternatively, the network position of the parietal target either generally or specific to a given task may be associated with its effective change in connectivity and/or behavior. Given that the authors have effects that are specific not only to target, but also differ as a function of task, I feel as though these data could be leveraged to provide substantial insights into what factors are critical for an effective intervention.

Relatedly, the authors offer conclusions in the discussion regarding what constitutes a successful intervention, but they are either unsubstantiated by the present data, or unclear. For example, they state on page 20, lines 439-441:

"It is the combination of a challenging task with concurrent brain stimulation over the relevant cortical circuits that facilitates fast learning, a paradigm amenable to promote plasticity."

Similar sentiments are echoed on page 20, lines 451-453. Absent examination of task data, the relevant cortical circuits for the studied tasks are unclear. Consider that in Figure 9, the temporal targeted tRNS seems to induce the most stimulation in occipital areas. I would expect occipital cortex to be extremely relevant for the studied tasks, yet stimulation over those areas did not improve performance. Moreover, the importance of stimulation concurrent with tasks cannot be concluded from these data since there were no conditions that had no tasks. The differential performance across the studied tasks may potentially be leveraged here, but at the moment, this conclusion does not follow from the data. Since the authors have data that can help speak to some of these issues, it seems pertinent to use them.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Attention network modulation via tRNS correlates with attention gain" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Richard Ivry (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been greatly improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below. Though these revisions are essential, the manuscript will not be sent out for another round of external reviews and can be handled editorially.

1. While the Bayesian analyses are nice, they do not address the point that the effect sizes are likely to be inflated given the sample size. The issue is that when sample size is small and reporting of results is conditioned on statistical significance (e.g. p< 0.05) , effect size will be inflated. This needs to be acknowledged in the discussion. See, for example, the reference below for more discussion of inflated effect sizes in studies with small samples.

Yarkoni, T. (2009). Big correlations in little studies: Inflated fMRI correlations reflect low statistical power-Commentary on Vul et al. (2009). Perspectives on psychological science, 4(3), 294-298.

2. Please report the analyses showing that the number of frames censored were similar across sessions in the manuscript.

3. The task-based univariate results are quite illuminating. It would seem pertinent to mention in the manuscript that both tasks activate IPS in the discussion of why effects were observed for the OD task but not the TOJ task.

results.result: The study implemented a 4-day cross-task training protocol with tRNS delivered to parietal cortex (IPS), hMT+, or sham, measuring behavioral and resting-state fMRI outcomes before and 24 hours after training in 30 healthy subjects.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C26, C27, C32, C33, C181-C186 collectively describe the experimental design, which is clearly documented with appropriate regulatory approval, sample size justification (after exclusions), and detailed stimulation parameters. The methodology is sufficiently rigorous for the study objectives.

results.result: Parietal tRNS during training produced significant improvement in orientation discrimination (OD) task performance (29.8% improvement, p=0.001) from pre- to post-test, while hMT+ and Sham groups showed no significant improvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C44 provide comprehensive statistical evidence including baseline equivalence (C35), significant interaction effects (C38), and post-hoc comparisons showing site-specific effects. The statistical approach is appropriate with effect sizes reported (Cohen's d values), supporting the conclusion of selective parietal effects.

results.result: No significant learning effects were observed for the temporal order judgment (TOJ) task across any stimulation condition from pre- to post-test, though parietal stimulation showed some effects during training sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 and C64-C69 demonstrate null results for TOJ task with appropriate statistical tests showing no interaction effects (C48, C69). The finding that parietal stimulation showed effects during training (C66) but not at post-test is internally consistent and properly documented with statistical comparisons.

results.result: During the 4-day training period, the parietal tRNS group showed progressive improvement in OD task performance, with significant divergence from control groups beginning on day 3 and sustained through day 4.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C63 and C120-C121 provide detailed time-course analysis with appropriate repeated measures ANOVA showing significant interaction effects (C51) and post-hoc comparisons at each time point. The cumulative learning pattern is well-documented with within-group comparisons (C60-C62) showing progressive improvement across all training days.

results.result: Parietal tRNS increased resting-state functional connectivity within the dorsal and ventral attention network (DVAN), with significant increases persisting 24 hours after the final training session, while hMT+ and Sham conditions showed decreased connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C83 demonstrate rigorous fMRI analysis with appropriate quality control (C70), baseline equivalence (C71), and significant interaction effects (C74). The finding is supported by both network-level (C73-C83) and node-by-node analyses (addressed in later claims), with proper statistical corrections and effect sizes reported.

results.result: Node-by-node analysis of DVAN connectivity confirmed network-wide increases in functional connectivity after parietal stimulation, with stronger positive correlations between all node pairs, while hMT+ and Sham showed decreased connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C95 provide complementary analysis to the network-level findings, using all ROI pairs as individual observations. The significant interaction effect (C86) and post-hoc comparisons (C87-C93) with appropriate corrections for variance inhomogeneity strengthen the main connectivity findings. The consistency between network-level and node-level analyses supports the robustness of the results.

results.result: The default mode network (DMN) showed no significant changes in functional connectivity following any stimulation condition, demonstrating network specificity of the parietal tRNS effects on the DVAN.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C107 provide critical control analyses showing no effects on DMN (C96-C98, C104-C106) and significant network × condition interaction (C99), demonstrating that connectivity changes were specific to the task-relevant DVAN rather than global or non-specific effects. This specificity is essential for interpreting the DVAN findings as functionally meaningful.

results.result: Behavioral improvement in the OD task positively correlated with increased DVAN functional connectivity (r=0.44, p=0.022 for post-test; r=0.48, p=0.012 for training improvement), with effects persisting 24 hours after stimulation ended.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 report brain-behavior correlations with modest effect sizes (R²=0.2-0.23). While statistically significant, the authors acknowledge potential inflation of effect sizes due to small sample size (C170-C171). The correlations support the functional relevance of connectivity changes but require replication in larger samples for confident interpretation.

results.result: The study concludes that parietal tRNS coupled with training modulates large-scale cortical dynamics by strengthening functionally selective neural pathways, with connectivity changes serving as a marker for enduring behavioral effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 and C7 synthesize the main findings linking behavior and connectivity. The conclusion is supported by the convergence of behavioral improvements (C39), connectivity increases (C74-C83), and brain-behavior correlations (C108-C113), though the mechanistic interpretation (C116-C117) involves some inference beyond the direct data.

results.result: Stimulation site selection within a network is crucial for successful augmentation, with effects specific to parietal cortex and not spreading to anatomically proximate but functionally distinct regions like hMT+.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131 are well-supported by the site-specific behavioral effects (C39-C44) and the lack of effects with hMT+ stimulation despite anatomical proximity. The inclusion of hMT+ as an active control strengthens the conclusion that effects depend on functional network properties rather than just current delivery.

results.result: The selective improvement in OD but not TOJ task, despite identical visual stimuli, is consistent with cross-task training paradigms and may reflect competition between cortical representations requiring different perceptual weightings.
results.evaluation: Claims C122, C135-C139 provide a theoretically grounded interpretation of task-selective learning, supported by citations to similar findings (C135) and theoretical models (C137). The interpretation is speculative (C136-C137) but consistent with the data showing OD-specific improvements (C39) and the cross-task training design (C26).

results.result: Task-evoked fMRI analysis showed that OD and TOJ tasks activated similar cortical regions at baseline, but behavioral gains differed dramatically, indicating that stimulus-evoked activity alone does not predict learning-critical regions and that network connectivity changes are more informative.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C153 integrate task-based fMRI (C148) with electric field modeling (C147) and connectivity findings (C152) to argue that network dynamics rather than regional activation predict learning. The logic is sound and supported by the dissociation between similar activation patterns (C148) and different behavioral outcomes (C149), though the interpretation involves inference (C150, C153).

results.result: Bilateral parietal tRNS modulated the entire attention network rather than producing only local changes, with effects being network-specific rather than spreading to neighboring regions or networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C165 are supported by the widespread connectivity increases within DVAN (C83, C94), lack of DMN changes (C96-C98), and absence of IPS modulation with hMT+ stimulation (C165). The conclusion of network-wide but selective effects is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Learning of the visuospatial attention task was achieved within four short training sessions, with effects persisting at least 24 hours after stimulation ended, confirming and extending previous findings on tRNS efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 and C123 summarize the temporal characteristics of learning, supported by the pre-post behavioral data (C39) and the persistence of both behavioral (C39) and connectivity (C75) changes 24 hours post-training. The comparison to previous work (C123, C127) appropriately contextualizes the findings.

results.result: The study proposes that functional connectivity changes following parietal stimulation affected behavior through rapid modulation of network connectivity, potentially via temporal summation and stochastic resonance mechanisms that increase synchrony across large-scale functional systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C176 propose mechanistic explanations for the observed effects, but these are largely speculative (C172, C174) and based on theoretical frameworks from other studies (C173, C175). While the proposed mechanisms are plausible and supported by citations, they go beyond what can be directly tested with the current data.

results.result: The study employed methodological features to maximize task engagement, including individually tailored difficulty and random task alternation, which may have contributed to the observed learning effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C157 describe methodological features supported by citations (C154-C155) and clearly documented in the methods. The speculation about task alternation forcing resource allocation (C157) is reasonable but not directly tested. These features strengthen the experimental design.

results.result: The study acknowledges a limitation of relatively small sample size (n=10 per group) which may inflate effect sizes in brain-behavior correlations.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C171 appropriately acknowledge a key limitation with supporting citation (C171). This transparency is important for interpreting the correlation results (C108-C113) and indicates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The study concludes that tRNS can efficiently promote behavioral improvements and speed up learning by modulating task-related neural networks, opening a critical window for cortical plasticity with potential clinical applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C180 and C8 present broad conclusions and speculations about clinical applications. While C177 is supported by the data, claims about this being the 'first study' (C178), opening 'critical windows' (C179), and clinical benefits (C180, C8) are speculative and go beyond what the current healthy-subject data can support. Clinical efficacy requires direct testing in patient populations.
